title: Everything you need to know about Fine-tuning and Merging LLMs: Maxime Labonne
talk_summary: Maxime Labonne explains the LLM training lifecycle (pretraining, SFT, preference alignment), when fine-tuning is worth it versus prompt engineering, how to build SFT datasets, and model-merging techniques (SLERP, DARE, passthrough, Franken-MoE) that combine fine-tuned weights without GPUs. It is a tutorial on training/merging open-weight models, not on running agent systems.

takeaways.what_they_do: Before considering fine-tuning, build a robust evaluation structure with multiple metrics (accuracy, cost, latency) or a custom benchmark for niche use cases, and reuse it to evaluate any new model.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the idea is to have a really robust evaluation uh structure where you have a lot of different metrics that you're interested in

takeaways.what_they_do: Filter training/eval samples with rule-based filters plus reward models or LLM-as-judge to remove low-quality samples, and dedupe exact and fuzzy duplicates.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can also use more clever techniques like reward models or LM as a judge to evaluate the quality of each sample and filter out the bad samples

takeaways.technique: Synthetic data generated by frontier models
takeaways.what_they_do: Most SFT datasets use synthetic data generated with frontier models, which they call a great way to build higher-quality datasets than human-written ones.
takeaways.evidence_quote: most sft data set I want you to say that use synthetic data and that's perfectly fine usually it's generated with Frontier models

takeaways.what_they_do: Merge weights of different fine-tuned models (SLERP, DARE, passthrough, Franken-MoE) to combine capabilities; requires no GPU and produced top open-leaderboard 7B models.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it doesn't required any GPU so it's super efficient and it provides excellent results
takeaways.numbers: entire top eight or top 10 of 7B Open LLM Leaderboard v1 were merge models
